title: Two Ships Sink Near Strait of Hormuz as Attacks on Vessels Intensify
excerpt: The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after a projectile strike and fire, while the bulk carrier Cape Dao, hit on September 23, was reported sinking after a failed rescue attempt.
body:
• The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank in the Strait of Hormuz after sustaining damage and a fire; all 21 crew members were safely evacuated with no injuries reported.
  • The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao, struck by a projectile on September 23, was reported sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt.
  • Maritime officials say attacks around the strait have increased over the past 10 days, as Iran says it is intensifying strikes in response to a US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions.
  • About a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war, making each new attack a direct risk to energy prices worldwide.

Two commercial vessels have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in separate projectile attacks, maritime officials said on Wednesday, as strikes on shipping through the world's most important energy waterway intensify. The losses mark a further escalation in a campaign that has steadily widened from tankers to cargo and container ships.

The GFS Pride, a Singapore-flagged container ship with capacity for 2,824 twenty-foot equivalent units, went down while transiting the strait, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA). In a statement cited by Reuters, the authority said the vessel sustained damage and a fire on board before it sank. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported.

"GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated."

— Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore

A second vessel lost weeks after it was hit

In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged dry bulk carrier Cape Dao sank near the strait weeks after it was struck by a projectile on September 23, according to data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the UN shipping agency. Maritime sources said one crew member was killed in that attack, while the remaining crew were evacuated shortly after the vessel was hit. British maritime risk group Vanguard said the Cape Dao was reported sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt.

https://x.com/visionergeo/status/2110379001441140994

Pakistan's Hydrographer issued a navigational warning dated October 14 cautioning mariners about the GFS Pride, reporting the vessel sunk with floating containers in the water — a hazard for any ship still attempting the passage.

An analysis of IMO casualty data showed the two vessels were among the very few to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28. Reuters, citing the same IMO data, described the GFS Pride as the second vessel to sink since the war started, with the Cape Dao following as its condition deteriorated.

Singapore condemns the attacks

Singapore's maritime authority condemned the strikes in direct terms. "MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law," the authority said. The managers of both vessels — UAE-based GFS Ship Management FZE for the GFS Pride and Peonies Shipmanagement FZE for the Cape Dao — could not immediately be reached for comment, Reuters reported.

Why the strait matters

The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war. Tehran has sought to tighten its control over the strait since US and Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, restricting transit to gain leverage over Washington.

Attacks around the strait have increased over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is intensifying strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month. Two senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Iran is increasingly using new tactics to target vessels passing through the strait, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and influence the US midterm elections. While Iran and the US have primarily targeted tankers, cargo and container vessels have also come under attack, been immobilised or sunk.

What it means for India and the diaspora

India imports the bulk of its crude oil, and Gulf routes remain central to that supply even after diversification. Sustained attacks on Hormuz shipping push up crude prices, freight rates and insurance premiums — costs that show up for diaspora households as dearer fuel, higher airfares on Gulf routes and, if the disruption deepens, renewed inflation pressure in both India and the Gulf states where millions of Indian workers live.

What happens next

Shipping lines must now decide whether the strait remains passable at acceptable risk. Each additional sinking raises war-risk insurance costs and strengthens the case for rerouting, naval escorts or a negotiated transit arrangement. For now, maritime authorities are warning vessels in the area, and the count of ships lost since February continues to climb.
